turns.t: Good afternoon, doctor. Sorry we're a bit damp, the rain came down just as we got out of the car. And the parking, my goodness, we went round three times.
It's always like that when the weather turns, I'm afraid. Please, come in, everyone sit down. Mrs. Rao, you take the chair by the desk. And who have you brought with you?

This is my daughter Meera, and this is Lakshmi, she stays with me and helps in the house. I told them both I'm fine, but they insisted. Now I'm worried it's something serious, why else would they insist?
Madam, we only insisted because of the nights. You have been crying out when you turn in bed.
That's helpful, Lakshmi. Mrs. Rao, tell me what's been happening, in your own words first.
My right shoulder, doctor. It is paining so much, mostly at night. When I lie on that side it wakes me up, and in the day I cannot even reach the top shelf in the kitchen.
And how long has this been going on?
About four months, no, five. Meera, is it four or five?
It started just after Diwali, Mummy, so it is nearer four. But it has gotten much worse in the last month, doctor. She can't comb her hair on that side, or fasten her blouse.
Four months, then, worsening. Mrs. Rao, how bad is the pain at its worst, would you call it mild, moderate or severe?
Severe at night. In the day it is moderate. Is it a cancer? Everyone on my WhatsApp group says shoulder pain means the heart.
I understand why you'd worry, and I'll come to that. Let me ask a few questions first. Have you had any fall or injury to the shoulder?
No, no fall. I have been very careful, Lakshmi holds my arm even to go to the bathroom.
Any fever, or feeling hot and unwell?
No fever, doctor.
And any numbness or tingling down the arm into the hand?
No numbness. Only the pain, and that stiffness.
Good. Let me ask about your health generally. Are there any long-term conditions I should know about?
Sugar. I have had diabetes for fifteen years now.
That's relevant, actually, I'll explain why shortly. And have you had any operations in the past?
They took out my gallbladder, ten years ago. In Hyderabad. Nothing since.
Thank you. Now, which medicines are you taking at present?

Let me think, there is the sugar tablet, metformin, 500 mg, twice a day after food. Then the paracetamol, 500 mg, I take it at night for the shoulder, but it hardly helps. And, Lakshmi, what was the third? The vitamin.
The vitamin D, madam, one sachet on Sundays.
Let me check your blood pressure and pulse first. Blood pressure is 136 over 84, and pulse is 74.

That's a little on the upper side, but not worrying today. Now I'd like to examine the shoulder. Lakshmi, could you help your madam out of her cardigan? Mrs. Rao, I'm going to lift your arm gently and tell me when it hurts.
Ow, ow, there. That is the place, doctor. Stop, stop, please.
I'm so sorry, that's enough. Now let me try from behind. Can you lift the other arm the same way?
This one goes up easily. See, it goes all the way.

It does. Right, you can put the cardigan back on. What I found is that the right shoulder is very stiff, and you can only lift it up to about shoulder height, whether I move it or you do. The other shoulder moves freely.
What is it, doctor? Please say it quickly, I have been thinking all kinds of things.
This looks most likely like a frozen shoulder. It's more common in people with diabetes, and it commonly hurts most at night. It isn't cancer, and it isn't your heart.
Oh, thank God. Meera, did you hear? It is not the cancer.
I heard, Mummy. How long does it take to go away, doctor?
It's a slow condition, I'll be honest. It can take many months, even a year or more, but it does get better on its own, and we can make it easier.
A year? What can I do in the meantime? I cannot sleep.

I'm going to refer you to a physiotherapist who will teach you gentle stretches, which are the mainstay of treatment. In the meantime, a warm towel on the shoulder before bed, and sleep with a pillow tucked under that arm.
I can do the hot towel every night, doctor. And I will learn the stretches also.
Wonderful. Mrs. Rao, keep the paracetamol going at night as you are.
And no injection? My neighbour had an injection.
We can talk about that later if the physiotherapy isn't enough, but not today.
All right. When will I see you again?
I'd like to see you again in six weeks to see how the stiffness is moving.
We'll book it at the desk on the way out, Mummy. Thank you, doctor, and sorry again about the rain on your floor.
Not at all. Take care, all of you.

physical_examination.normalized_finding: Restricted right shoulder range of motion

clinical_assessment.assessment: most likely like a frozen shoulder

clinical_actions.description: Warm towel on the shoulder before bed, pillow under the arm, continue paracetamol at night
